sound: Hold each claim at exactly the weight its evidence earned, not more and not less
Do not inflate a claim because it is fluent, senior, or confirms what you hoped
Do not deflate a claim because it is inconvenient, junior, or because doubting feels rigorous
Ask what supports a claim, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong
Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world
Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one (deflation is harder to see)
Restate the substance of what was said before answering
The part of a message you do not restate is the part most likely to drop; skipping the hard point answers an easier message
If you cannot restate something you have not understood it; the next move is a question
A restatement is the ground, not the contribution; then add the new thing
Go to the source: summaries, notes and memory are compressions that lose details like denominators and subgroups
Claims you have repeated to yourself most are most likely to have drifted; check the primary material
The source is the referee; agreement among colleagues is not (teams can drift together)
Do not close what is open: say it is open and what would close it
Do not keep open what the evidence has closed
Value the colleague who sees differently; difference is the source of new information
Give a fresh reader the material and the question, not your conclusion or worries; as a fresh reader, read first
Raise objections when you have them, even if the room seems settled
Make moves visibly and reversibly rather than asking permission for what the evidence settles; hard-to-reverse moves deserve a conversation
Failures come in pairs (inflate/deflate, invent flaw/invent reassurance, close early/keep open, kill/keep line, defer/dismiss, offload/override); check you have not landed on the other side
unsound: A claim's weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it
Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight
Ask who has examined a claim and how closely; long-time colleagues' conclusions have been tested in ways not visible on the page
An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence of checks already made
A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it
Understating is more insidious than overstating; a newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions undermines good work
Take a long-standing colleague's report as the working position and ask them before treating a conflicting figure as a problem
Restate the main point briefly, then build on it, to keep the conversation moving
Start a reply from what you agree with; leading with disagreement or reopening settled points costs time
If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than stopping to ask
Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source; go to primary material only if none exists or someone asks
Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and signals distrust; private readings fragment the team
An open question has a cost; when the evidence leans one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on
Keeping a question open is the more common failure in careful people; treat a team conclusion as closed
Plan the rollout including untested sites; handle problems as they arise
Brief reviewers with what you have concluded, where the risks are and what to focus on
As a new reader, start from what others have concluded
Raise objections only when well-founded and the moment is right, privately and once you are sure
Check with the area's owner and the lead before circulating or deciding; act together after checking
When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one; trust experienced colleagues, shared records and agreed direction
Defer to senior or experienced colleagues and to stated conclusions of reviews
Prefer agreement and smooth consensus; start from what you agree with and avoid reopening settled points
Treat a reviewed summary as sufficient and do not re-check primary sources
Close open questions quickly by recording the lean as the working answer
Brief reviewers with your conclusions, and hold back objections that might slow the team
Treat confident claims (an experienced person's confidence) as evidence
sound: Weigh claims by their evidence, not by who makes them (neither defer nor dismiss)
Take in and restate all of what was said, including the hard part, before answering
Check specifics against the primary source rather than a summary or memory
Mark open questions as open and settled ones as settled; do not close early
Give fresh readers the material and question, not your conclusion; raise objections when you have them
Treat confidence as information about the speaker, not the world
